video_title: Mercor Raises $750M at $20B Valuation | CEO Brendan Foody
gist: Mercor CEO Brendan Foody explains how Mercor sells RL environments (apps, worlds, rubric-graded tasks) built by its 5M-expert network to AI labs, argues Jevons paradox makes human training data demand grow rather than shrink until superintelligence, and predicts every Fortune 500 firm will train sovereign models with eval spend scaling by inference budget. The $750M raise/$20B valuation in the title is not discussed in the transcript.

insights.claim: Mercor grew revenue more than 5x on a nine-figure basis in roughly a year since September of the prior year.
insights.speaker: Brendan Foody
insights.so_what: Hypergrowth at nine-figure scale supports premium private valuations for AI training-data vendors.
insights.quote: So we grew more than 5 times, yes, on a nine- figure basis.

insights.claim: Mercor's talent platform has over 5 million people looking for work and pays out over $4-5 million per day to experts, versus about $1 million per year 24 months earlier.
insights.speaker: Brendan Foody
insights.so_what: Expert payouts are a proxy for lab spend on human data; the trajectory signals exploding demand for RL training data.
insights.quote: 24 months ago, we were paying out a million dollars a year

insights.claim: Mercor has paid out almost $1 billion to experts historically, runs payouts on Stripe Connect, and has conducted over 7 million AI-driven interviews.
insights.speaker: Brendan Foody
insights.so_what: Cumulative payout and interview volume quantify Mercor's data moat in expert vetting.

insights.claim: About 70% of Mercor's experts arrive via referrals, which Foody says produce the highest-quality talent and create network effects for mobilizing doctors, lawyers and engineers.
insights.speaker: Brendan Foody
insights.so_what: Referral-driven supply lowers acquisition cost and strengthens network-effect defensibility.

insights.claim: Foody says Mercor created 'the fastest growing job category in history' — people training AI models — and found the market before competing talent networks.
insights.speaker: Brendan Foody
insights.so_what: Human-data labor for AI is an emerging, large employment category worth tracking as a labor-market and investment theme.

insights.claim: Mercor does not plan to IPO in the next 12 months, but an IPO is 'definitely on our radar'.
insights.speaker: Brendan Foody
insights.so_what: Pushes any public-market access to Mercor beyond late 2027; private secondary/venture vehicles remain the only exposure.
insights.quote: So we're not looking to go public in the next 12 months, but it's definitely on our radar.

insights.claim: Mercor operates three products: a talent platform, Studio (an AI-copiloted data platform where experts build RL environments), and an AI project manager where agents autonomously hire, manage and grade experts.
insights.speaker: Brendan Foody
insights.so_what: Automating project management with agents expands margins versus labor-heavy data-labeling peers.

insights.claim: Foody argues Mercor is not a marketplace taking a GMV fee like Uber; experts are one ingredient in the RL-environment datasets it sells to AI labs.
insights.speaker: Brendan Foody
insights.so_what: Valuing Mercor on marketplace take-rate metrics may misprice it; it should be viewed as a data/product vendor.
insights.quote: the biggest misconception about the business is that people think of us as a marketplace, like Uber

insights.claim: An RL environment has three parts: apps (clones of Google Workspace, Salesforce, Adobe etc.), worlds (the content inside the apps like messages, slides, documents), and tasks (prompts plus rubrics that grade model attempts).
insights.speaker: Brendan Foody
insights.so_what: A useful taxonomy for evaluating RL-environment startups and where each captures value.

insights.claim: Mercor acquired Deep Tune, an app-clone builder that had just raised a Series A from A16Z, because building app clones was Mercor's biggest bottleneck; a lab client had proactively recommended Deep Tune as its app partner.
insights.speaker: Brendan Foody
insights.so_what: Signals consolidation in the RL-environment supply chain; app-clone builders are attractive M&A targets.

insights.claim: Deep Tune was Mercor's second acquisition after Seople, and Foody says Mercor is exploring additional M&A categories.
insights.speaker: Brendan Foody
insights.so_what: Expect further roll-up activity by well-capitalized AI data vendors.

insights.claim: Mercor built its own payments operation after a competitor's payment failures left over 1,000 workers Mercor had supplied unpaid, which catalyzed Mercor contracting directly with labs.
insights.speaker: Brendan Foody
insights.so_what: Payment reliability and direct lab relationships are competitive differentiators in expert-labor supply.

insights.claim: AI copilots let experts produce 3-5x more model-improvement output per hour, and per Jevons paradox this has made demand for human training data grow exponentially rather than shrink.
insights.speaker: Brendan Foody
insights.so_what: Bears assuming AI efficiency kills human-data demand may be wrong; volume growth can outrun productivity gains.
insights.quote: in the case of Jevons' paradox, demand just grew exponentially

insights.claim: Foody estimates about 99% of knowledge still lives in people's heads, so the human-to-model teaching market is bounded only by what humans can do that models cannot.
insights.speaker: Brendan Foody
insights.so_what: The addressable market for expert data persists until superintelligence; timing that is the key risk variable.

insights.claim: Foody counters the 'short-lived category' bear case: the market lasts as long as superintelligence is not reached, because models need human feedback at the frontier much like students need a teacher to grade essays.
insights.speaker: Brendan Foody
insights.so_what: Duration of human-data demand is tied to AGI timelines; leading lab researchers expect this training mode for the next decade.

insights.claim: Foody says many top Silicon Valley VCs passed early believing the human-data market would disappear within a few years, and that this mispricing kept competition lower than in foundation models.
insights.speaker: Brendan Foody
insights.so_what: Consensus skepticism created a less competitive market; Foody thinks it is now near consensus, which could compress that edge.
insights.quote: a lot of the top firms in Silicon Valley just thought the market would disappear within a few years

insights.claim: Foody says data is mispriced versus compute and algorithms in the AI-progress stack because investors assume superintelligence in about three years.
insights.speaker: Brendan Foody
insights.so_what: If data is undervalued relative to compute, data vendors may offer asymmetric upside versus GPU plays.

insights.claim: Frontier labs are exponentially increasing their investment in RL environments, and most training compute now goes to RL rather than pretraining or SFT.
insights.speaker: Brendan Foody
insights.so_what: Rising RL spend is a direct demand driver for expert-data and environment vendors.

insights.claim: Foody's framework: frontier labs (Anthropic, OpenAI), inference providers (Fireworks, Base10) and application companies (Harvey) each face commoditization of large portions of their businesses.
insights.speaker: Brendan Foody
insights.so_what: Investors should underwrite each layer on its specific durable moat rather than revenue growth alone.

insights.claim: Application-layer AI moats are brand and data — specifically learning the distribution of what customers care about to build benchmarks and training datasets, not training on customer data.
insights.speaker: Brendan Foody
insights.so_what: Screen app-layer AI names for proprietary eval/benchmark pipelines and brand strength.

insights.claim: Frontier labs' moat is mainly economies of scale in compute and RL data plus some recursive self-improvement, which Foody expects will not be a vertical takeoff.
insights.speaker: Brendan Foody
insights.so_what: Scale advantages favor the largest labs; skeptical of fast-takeoff narratives.

insights.claim: Inference providers reselling GPUs have zero switching costs; durable value comes from building custom models for customers that cannot be moved to other infrastructure, which Fireworks does well.
insights.speaker: Brendan Foody
insights.so_what: Favor inference providers with custom-model lock-in over pure GPU resellers.
insights.quote: the switching costs from reselling GPUs are zero

insights.claim: Foody believes investors overestimate the revenue quality of some API businesses because API switching costs are so low; Mercor itself switches models daily based on evals.
insights.speaker: Brendan Foody
insights.so_what: Discount API-revenue multiples for model providers lacking lock-in.
insights.quote: investors are overestimating the quality of the revenues of some API businesses

insights.claim: Foody thinks Anthropic and OpenAI could each become companies worth over $10 trillion.
insights.speaker: Brendan Foody
insights.so_what: Extremely bullish framing on frontier-lab terminal value from a key supplier.
insights.quote: I think both of them could very well be companies worth over $10 trillion

insights.claim: Advanced labs are a leading indicator for AI-native companies like Harvey, which are in turn a leading indicator for enterprises; vertical AI firms must build cutting-edge models in their domain because 'a model is a product'.
insights.speaker: Brendan Foody
insights.so_what: Watch frontier-lab practices to anticipate enterprise AI spending patterns 1-2 cycles later.

insights.claim: Mercor has published public legal benchmarks including APEX and APEX Agents and works with Harvey on post-training data.
insights.speaker: Brendan Foody
insights.so_what: Benchmark ownership gives data vendors influence over how vertical AI progress is measured.

insights.claim: Foody predicts every Fortune 500 company will become like a 'Neolab', using employees and contractors to curate evaluation tasks and train their own models as human processes become agent-based.
insights.speaker: Brendan Foody
insights.so_what: Opens a large enterprise TAM for eval/RL-data vendors beyond frontier labs; Foody says it is the 'first inning'.

insights.claim: Enterprises like Goldman Sachs will not let frontier labs train on their proprietary data because it would be like sharing competitive advantages with a competitor, so they will build their own models — the AI data sovereignty theme also championed by Jensen, Alex Karp and Satya.
insights.speaker: Brendan Foody
insights.so_what: Undercuts lab pitches of enterprise data flywheels; bullish for sovereign-AI tooling and custom-model vendors.

insights.claim: Inference-spend heuristic: under $10M/year enterprises barely care about evals; at $10-100M about 10% of inference budget should go to evaluation datasets; above $100M (e.g. Harvey, Casetext) custom post-training becomes economical by amortizing fixed training costs over inference.
insights.speaker: Brendan Foody
insights.so_what: Track enterprise inference spend tiers to forecast demand for eval and post-training services.

insights.claim: Mercor itself spends almost $1 million per day on inference.
insights.speaker: Brendan Foody
insights.so_what: Illustrates how fast AI-native firms scale inference bills, a demand signal for model providers.
insights.quote: we spend almost a million dollars a day on logical deduction

insights.claim: Foody's two pieces of advice for enterprises: create tasks with clear rubric-based assessments rather than assuming models learn by reading documents, and start with evaluation as the foundation.
insights.speaker: Brendan Foody
insights.so_what: Enterprises with mature eval practices are better positioned to capture AI value.

insights.claim: Foody expects non-tech Fortune 50 companies to wake up as inference bills mature, since some face existential threats from frontier models entering their sectors.
insights.speaker: Brendan Foody
insights.so_what: Incumbents in sectors targeted by frontier labs may face disruption; watch for defensive AI spend.

insights.claim: Scale's Meta deal moved Alex and the core team to Meta while Scale refocused most of its business on Meta; Foody says Mercor would never do a similar deal and has turned down chances to cash out.
insights.speaker: Brendan Foody
insights.so_what: Competitive vacuum after Scale's Meta tie-up benefited independent data vendors like Mercor.

insights.claim: Many early Mercor customers were startups, about 80% of which went bankrupt within 12 months, though some like Cognition became large.
insights.speaker: Brendan Foody
insights.so_what: Early-stage AI customer churn is extreme; customer concentration shifted to labs over time.

insights.claim: Foody proposes eliminating federal taxes for the bottom half of Americans (under ~$70,000), who contribute about 3% of federal tax revenue, to stimulate job creation; Jeff Bezos engaged with the idea on X.
insights.speaker: Brendan Foody
insights.so_what: Policy idea with labor-market implications; low market relevance near term.
insights.quote: The bottom half of Americans account for 3% of the federal government's tax revenue

insights.claim: Foody notes AI companies including Mercor are hiring as fast as they can despite narratives that AI will eliminate jobs.
insights.speaker: Brendan Foody
insights.so_what: Near-term AI labor displacement narratives may be overstated relative to AI-sector hiring.
